utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, the Chamber was kept busy with an urgent matter, which did not allow any further delay and that caused the late start this afternoon. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Theunens, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before we pick up where we left off on Friday, I would like to see if you can help us with respect to a document already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit D182 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this question I'm asking you based not only the fact that you've reviewed documents, but also that you worked in UNPF at the time, so you may be able to assist us with the identity of a particular person. This is a document that both the Prosecution and the Defence stipulate has the wrong date on it. It should be dated 4 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could get the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll see that it's sent from Knin by a Colonel Ratsouk. Can you tell us and help us understand who Colonel Ratsouk was?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a Colonel Ratsouk who when I arrived at the -- it was still called UNCRO headquarters in December 1994 -- was working in the office called CMNAT, and I think that stands for chief military negotiation an analysis team, and he was working there together -- or I think he was a deputy to a Belgian Brigadier, Pierre Peeters now in what position Ratsouk was in Knin in August 1995, I'm not sure. I know he had to leave the UNPROFOR headquarters in January or February of 1995, and my understanding was that he was sent to the headquarters of Sector East. He returned to the UNPF headquarters, but I don't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, in fact, Colonel Ratsouk was member of UN Sector South on the 4th of August, or was he affiliated UNPF or UNCRO in Zagreb at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell. So it could be that UNPF headquarters dispatched him for a certain time-period to Sector South, but I have no further information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to where we left off on Friday, I would like to show you an exhibit which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is 1D63-0218, please. Mr. President, is not yet ready to be released, do we'll show it via Sanction or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You recall we were talking about the 134th Home Guard's Brigade at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is a report dated 21 August 1995 about -- which was a list that was prepared of participants in Operation Storm of the 134th Home Guard Regiment. And you will see there at the bottom -- if we could actually turn the page. The last sentence there says: "The 134th Home Guard Regiment has a total of 2302 members on its list." That's as of 21 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. And when we see the document we also see that the 134th Home Guard Regiment, like the other units, has its own artillery assets. For example, under heading 10 and 11, just to clarify a point that was discussed earlier during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go back to -- actually, Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D986 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 65 ter 1335, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You will recall, Mr. Theunens, that I took you through a series of documents at the end of the day on Friday about the commander of the 134th being unable to implement orders effectively, a problem with respect to burning and looting in that unit. That's what was in the operational diary for the 18th of August. Then subsequent orders to establish a check-point as well as to demobilize problem soldiers, including soldiers in the 134th. If we could turn here to page -- numbered page 37 in the English. This is the report of the inspection of the Split Military District from the 30th of October that was done by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think -- we showed the page on Friday, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I show the English translation is 26 pages, so we can't show page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it is numbered paragraph 3.1, so I may have an earlier draft translation. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now for the 134th, it says: "By the order of the defence minister, based on the proposal submitted by the operative group and the order of the Split Military District, the approved numerical strength of the regiment was 581 soldiers. After the demobilization the number fell to 579 and the regiment's structure was adapted accordingly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please. "According to the commander's order, the regiment sent 392 members on leave..." And then talks about the 187 are doing. Now based on the prior document I showed you, as well as this document, it would appear that between 21 August 1995 and 30 October 1995, 1,721 of the 134th Home Guard Regiment had been demobilized. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And of the remaining 581, 392 were sent on leave. So if we could turn now to the next page, please. Actually this is section 3.2, the proposed measures under section B at the Split Military District level, the last recommendation is: "Make the necessary training analysis, and in cooperation with the Split Military District, organise --" oh, sorry. It says: "In according with the requirements, take into consideration the demobilization of the unit retaining only the corps regiment command?" Now it would appear, Mr. Theunens, would it not, that since that report on 18 August about, the commander of the 134th Home Guard Regiment having difficulty implementing the orders of the operative group, the decision was implemented to essentially first get rid of 75 per cent of the soldiers in the unit, and then with a recommendation of getting demobilizing the entire unit except for the corps regiment command, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report on 18 August is a -- at D885, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. The SIS report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay. It's another document. Indeed we can see there is a demobilization or to a large extent of the 134th Home Guard Regiment. However, it is not clear why this demobilization is taking place. In relation to D885, I would like to add that the document which states that the commander can demobilize people at his own wish, in priority, those who are -- who don't behave in accordance with the Code of Discipline. That document was not indicate that dismissal is used as a disciplinary punishment, as it is specified in Article 13 of the Code of Discipline which is P1017.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to P1017 then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before we continue can you also make reference to page numbers for -- for example, 3.1 appears both on page 8 and on page 19. Apparently, you were referring to the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the numbering of this document is not in every respect conclusive. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, because I can't see the -- I don't have this copy. Page 20 is the recommendation to take into consideration the demobilization of the unit. And, Mr. President, I will be referring back to this document so I ask that it be marked, and I tender it received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your, Honours, that becomes Exhibit D987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D987 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P1007, please. And if we can go to Article 13, which I believe is probably page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could go back to -- I see what you're referring to, Mr. Theunens, and if we could back now -- scroll up, please, I believe Article 11 is there. Now, these measures, one of the measures that can be taken under Article 11, subpart 5, is termination status as active serviceman, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Article 11 refers to disciplinary punishments and not disciplinary measures. And there's a distinction. Disciplinary measures can be decided upon by a brigade commander and higher, and these disciplinary measures are also specified in the various Articles, whereas when you read the Code of Discipline, disciplinary punishments or sentences are actually of a more serious nature, and they are used in case of violations of discipline, i.e., what is described as more serious violations, whereas the breaches -- I mean, you have the breaches. Are you getting response of a breach, you get a disciplinary measure. In response of a violation, i.e., a more serious violation, you get disciplinary punishment. And disciplinary punishments are in my understanding, the prerogative of the disciplinary prosecutor and the disciplinary Court. And that can be also found in Articles 6 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Articles that talk about active duty servicemen, right? And what's the distinction between active duty servicemen and mobilised members of the Home Guard Regiment, if you know?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any distinction in relation to those categories which is relevant in the context of your question int he code of Discipline. But if you point me to an Article, then, of course, I'm willing to have a look at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll see if I can do that for you. But as of right now what I'm interested in is, at this moment, you're not aware of any distinction between active duty serviceman and mobilised soldiers, correct? Under the Code of Conduct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the context of the issues we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could now go back to D987, please. And if we could -- if we could now to section 7.1. It's page 14 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now talking about the situation in the 142nd Home Guard Regiment as found during the inspection. It gives the numbers present. There's only 337 left -- present, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That paragraph that begins: "Displaced persons from Drnis ..." It says: "Displaced persons from Drnis make up 70 per cent of this unit. They had suffered heavy losses ... the demobilization after Operation Storm went too fast, and it was impossible to make better preparations. The decline in the number of unit members should be approached in a much better way in the next demobilization. And this last sentence: "There is an certain degree of concern on the part of the members of this unit - displaced persons - about what to do after the - it says mobilisation; It should be demobilization - about what to do after the demobilisation, and some of them have little time to prepare their houses, find accommodations for their family, and work." Now, in your analysis of Split Military District, you were aware, were you aware you not, that mobilized soldiers, in many cases, were displaced persons whose only source of income was, in fact, from the HV and their service in the HV, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know in many cases, there were displaced persons, but I'm not familiar with the social system in Croatia as to know whether or not they received any kind of assistance when they were not mobilized. I know they were paid when they were mobilized, but I don't know about their financial status or social status when they are demobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have one moment. I have a hard time now because of the differences in the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's page 18 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now the proposed measures concerning the 113th Sibenik Motorised Brigade. And in contrast with the suggestion that the 134th be demobilized except for the corps command, this one has a recommendation: "Suggest that the Brigade be commended by the chief of the Main Staff for its distinguished and proper execution of tasks?" Now, there were, in fact, distinctions being made between units in this inspection, correct, in terms of some that he were being commended and others that were being suggested for total demobilization, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed we would have to see the reasons for this difference in -- in opinions that are expressed in relation to these units because whether -- whether the commendation has to do with the manner in which, for example, the records are kept or command and control is functioning at the time of the inspection or whether the commendation is related to other aspects is something that I would have to see in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that you cite in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but I haven't seen the page with reference to the 113th Brigade on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now go to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 7 in the English, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, it's page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now in the introductory section of the inspection, and at the top it says: "Planned inspections and controls of the liberated areas have not been fully established yet, but considerable progress has been achieved in the prevention of theft, destruction of houses, and similar, which should continue to be considered a priority and permanent task." Now, if we could go to the last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it should be the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll see that the report has as attachments, among other things, the last entry is -- an attachment is the inspection of political activities, and that, in fact, is Exhibit P1138.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have that. And if we can go to page 3 in the English, please. Actually, if we could scroll up. It may be the previous page; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this at the bottom of this under "Discipline and Order," you had highlighted this sentence that said: "Due to undisciplined conduct and in the absence of sanctions against what has occurred, the theft of property and arbitrary occupation of premises still persists and could cause wider political damage." Right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put the entire paragraph actually in my report on English page 353, so I -- maybe Mr. Waespi highlighted that sentence during my examination, but the entire paragraph under the heading "Discipline an Order" can be found on English page 353 of part 2 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the top it says -- the conclusion reached, however. It says, the among other things: "The problems troubling this Military District are no different from problems of other Military Districts." And my first question to you is: This was an attachment to an overall inspection was done by the HV Main Staff which had a conclusion which I have read to you now, which said that, in fact, progress was being made on the prevention of -- let me quote it correctly. "Considerable progress has been achieved in the prevention of theft, destruction of houses, and similar, which should be continued to be a priority and permanent tasks." Would you agree with me that the report you cited was, in fact, something that had been considered by the inspectors of the Main Staff, and they came to the conclusion that I've read out to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I mean, I believe that the report by the political department stands as it is. Now, whether anyone else looked at other aspects and took those to draw the conclusion you have cited, it's possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going back now to the 18th of August -- first of all, let me ask you from a military perspective and as someone who was in the military, whether it is the Belgian army, the US army, or the Croatian army, is there a certain stigma attached when a unit is disbanded?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything depends of the reasons why it was disbanded. If it is disbanded for disciplinary reasons, yes, indeed the senior NCOs and the members of the officer corps of that unit would be looked at in a probably negative way by other officers and NCOs in the military. But if is disbanded just as a result of cutting of budgets, for example, some people may even feel sorry for them. My unit was disbanded because of budgetary constraints in Belgium, and lots of efforts were being done to keep the name existing, and so on, and so on, and the traditions, but there was no question whatsoever of any stigmatization or other negative considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit P71 again, which is the operational diary. And if we could go, please, to page 115 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now going back, and he is now reporting at the meeting what was in the SIS report that I showed you where Colonel Fuzul says: "Lack of discipline among 134 Home Guard Regiment." Coric, whoever that is, reports that the order is issued to carry out the control and inventory in 134th Home Guard Regiment. Next entry is the military police: "Control in Otric area. The MP check-point was established. The burning of houses and killing of cattle is being continued." Now, Otric was an area that was being used as a staging area for combat activities in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I have no specific recollection, but if you say so, I'm willing to accept that. It depends also on the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends also obviously on the time. I guess this is still around the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: From an UNMO report, UNMO analysis which is Exhibit P176, at page 8, the UNMO analysis reported that in the entire Otric area, which includes Otic and all surrounding villages, there were a total of 70 destroyed houses and 16 partially damaged. And if I could call up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D63-0202, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You see where Strmica is and Otric is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the left there. Resanovci in Bosnia. You see that the brown line is the international border?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The blue line is the HVO line. The red line is the VRS line. When we're talking about Otric, we're talking about an area that was being used by the HV to resupply into Bosnia. If you follow -- you can't really see the roads here, but there is only one road that goes up into the Resanovci area. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on general terms, I'm familiar with the terrain, so I'm willing to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have this marked. I'm going to use this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D988 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to P71. Mr. Registrar, again, page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now at a meeting, I think you highlighted this in your direct or Mr. Waespi did. This is now the 19th of August and an entry at the very top of the page: "The problem is the 6th Home Guard Regiment that is burning down the houses in..." and it's written as Rasanovci; I believe it should be Resanovci. And then it goes on. Now, from the map that I just showed you and admitted into evidence, Resanovci is a village in Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Resanovci is a village in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your direct examination at page 12375 to 12376, you spoke about the importance of the war diary at lines 20 to 25. It says: "It includes all the information that is considered important in order to understand the development of the operations, as well as the orders that have been given, degree of implementation, as well as minutes of - or records, I apologise - records of meetings that are held at the command post." At page 12376 you said at lines 10 to 14 when discussing these meetings, you said: "Then the members of the subordinate units or other attendees will provide their views on operations they have conducted, proposals they may have for future operations, problems they have encountered, and all other issues that are considered relevant in the context of this command meeting." Now, Mr. Theunens, after that entry about Otric on the 18th, and the 134th, and the military police setting up a check-point, in the operational diary of the Split Military District, there are no further entries about any reports of burning, or looting problems on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look again at the diary. I don't know the diary by heart. Even if -- even if you're right, on the same page we see it in front of us, the assistant commander for political activities at the end of the page states: "Burning down of houses is a huge problem." He doesn't specify whether it is in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina. From my point of view, there is no distinction, whether it is -- it -- it's not the area where these -- these crimes are being committed that is important. It is important that the commander knows that subordinate units of his on -- still on the 18th, whereas we know from the diary that similar crimes are already perpetrated in Grahovo and Glamoc around the 28th July, that three or four weeks the same activities are still being done by units that are subordinated to him, and that is the key issue in my view for the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That may be your view, but I may have a different view later, so let me ask you again: When you were reviewing these materials, is it correct to is say, and if you need time during the break, that's fine, that in the Split Military District operational diary after the 18th of August, there's no reference to burning and looting taking place on the territory of the Republic of Croatia after the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm allowed so, I will check it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The same question, then, with respect to reports from the political affairs department. There are no additional reports from political affairs after the 18th of August about burning and looting taking place on the territory of the Republic of Croatia that go to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On English page 342, second part of the report, I have a reference to looting and arson in the municipalities of Glamoc and Grahovo which is indeed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it is not Croatia, but it is still units of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me before you -- let me get there first. Is it units of the Split Military District or units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should be more precise. It is units of OG North, whereby OG North is subordinated to General Gotovina. So it is indeed, it is not just Split Military District, but are also units of the HVO included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You say it is included, but does it specify whether the people doing the burning are members of the HVO or members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to look at the document, and that is 65 ter 3461. But in any event, what I included of that document in my report is also the following quotation that is that: "During the command briefing at the OG North forward command post, the detrimental effect of such behaviour for the 'Croatian people and the promotion of our state in the world' is emphasised." So even if it is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the person who mentions this information at the command briefing has the impression that these activities are detrimental to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify this further. The report you're citing is, first of all, not from a meeting of the Split Military District and does not concern burning on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report from the SIS operative team at OG North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Of the HVO, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it OG North, which is operating as a force under the command of General Gotovina, and OG North is the -- I just have to look at the date. OG North used to be known as OG Vrba, but on 18 August there has been an order by General Gotovina to rename the OGs. And that document is 65 ter 3361.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But the SIS group there, that report is sent to Mostar, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be possible. But as I pointed out later -- earlier, the commander should not be waiting for a SIS report to arrive on his desk in order to know what his forces are doing in his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Theunens, let me just see if can I cut to the chase here. Do you agree with me that this is not a report of burning and looting on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to my original question, which was: I take it from the fact that you pointed to this document, that you can't point to any political affairs or SIS report which says that there is burning and looting taking place on the territory of the Republic of Croatia by HV after the 18th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to -- to look at my report during the break before I give an answer to that question. If I'm allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Theunens, let me show you Exhibit P20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a witness statement that has been admitted into evidence by Mr. Edward Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 21 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we go to lines 17 to 24. He says in his statement -- and Mr. Flynn was the head of the human rights action team in Sector South after Operation Storm. And he says: "Considering the total number of houses that were destroyed by fire during the three weeks following 7th of August, it's, of course, very difficult to say, but in almost every village we visited, or, let's say in many villages we visited, that would be more accurate, at least half the buildings had been burned and the numbers easily and quickly exceeded 100 and 200. So I have no doubt that at least 500 structures must have been burned down during those few weeks. But when I think of the size of Sector South, it would seem to me that it -- may have been more than that, but I would feel very comfortable in saying at least 500 structures were burned."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Lines 29 to 30, he says: "When I mentioned that estimate of 500 houses destroyed, I'm referring to houses that were destroyed in the couple of weeks or two or three weeks after Operation Storm."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Lines 5 to 8 he says: "In the following period of two or three weeks, beginning around the 20th of August, the frequency of burning buildings was reduced, but we were still struck by the fact that every day more buildings were seen to be on fire, and it seemed that some other areas were being targeted that had not been targeted earlier." Now, Mr. Flynn, just for the record, also testified in this case, at trial transcript 1314, lines 9 to 17, in similar terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go ... Mr. Registrar, if I could please have 65 ter 5658, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is a report that's sent to Josko Moric from the chief of the Split-Dalmatia police administration, Ivo Cipci. This is a report dated 24 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He writes at point 2: "From receipt of your previous telegram (18 August 1995) no cases of burning and destruction of houses in the aforementioned area were recorded." Then he talks about thefts, some of the perpetrators in three cases were HV members, were turned over to the military police. Six cases of the goods were confiscated, and criminal report was submitted against the perpetrators. Now, we're going to talk, Mr. Theunens, about Bosnia, but you reach a conclusion in your report, and by the way, I noted that having reviewed the first draft that you submitted to OTP in March of 2007, you did not include a conclusion or an opinion that the number and frequency of General Gotovina's orders indicated that the orders were not effective. And then -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I answer to that or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll pose a question. I will allow you to answer the question. Just let me complete the question, if you would. I'll show you a portion of -- via Sanction a portion of the pre-trial brief that was filed by the Prosecution after you submitted your initial report. There is paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, there was no submission of the official report. As we all know it was a first draft was sent to the -- to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He submitted a draft so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At 62, then, the Prosecution filed its pre-trial brief on the 17th of March, 2007, which had a conclusion at paragraph 62 that General Gotovina issued a number of orders between 4 August and 18 August "... that criminal activities cease and that disciplinary measures be taken, yet he failed to implement these orders to reign in the widespread lawful acts of his subordinate." Then the General Gotovina Defence filed a defence brief that commented on that. I noted in your April draft of the 2007 is the first time then that you include a conclusion that the number and frequency of the orders indicated that they lacked effectiveness. Did that conclusion -- was that impacted by the Prosecution's pre-trial brief and the Defence position -- I know you at least read the Defence brief. Did you conclude that conclusion because you had seen argument about it in the pre-trial briefs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you wanted, can I elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Mr. Misetic whether he seeks any further elaboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, my question to you is this, and can you look at that time during the break, but you reached this conclusion that the number of orders indicates that they lack effectiveness, and you base that on the fact that he issued additional orders on the same subject. However, if after -- if on the 18th of August orders are issued, and after the 18th of August, there are no additional reports to General Gotovina or the Split Military District Command about burning and looting in the territory, and there are no orders from General Gotovina regarding burning and looting and discipline in the liberated territory, isn't it the case, then, then all those orders together culminating on the 18th of August were effective, if I were to follow the logic that you used in concluding that they were ineffective?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because From the review did - and I can point you to these documents - there are still orders being issued after the 18 August and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let him finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While reviewing that material, I did not make a specific distinction as to whether these orders applied to Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia. From the point of view, from my point of view, the fact that these orders were issued by units, be it Operational Groups or their subordinate units, subordinated to General Gotovina independently or whether they were majority HV or HVO, the fact that these orders continued to be issued, as well as there continued to be reports, maybe not in Croatia but at least in other areas where these units were active, to me showed or indicated that indeed these orders lacked effectiveness. Just to finalise, in relation to the 134th Brigade we have -- Home Guard Regiment, 134th Home Guard Regiment we have been discussing at length, General Gotovina knew at the latest on the 6th of August that there were problems with the 134th Home Guard Regiment in Benkovac. So the fact that this unit around the 18th August again, based on the report we discussed, is involved in activities like burning and looting, in my view, shows that there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you used the word "problems," but you used that very vaguely when you say "problems in Benkovac." Tell me specifically what Mr. Grncaric reported as the problems in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Benkovac is discussed on -- starting on page 325. I will just take maybe 65 ter 2471 which is discussed on English page 328. I don't know whether you want me to read out what Grncaric reported to Major Juric, but I think -- I will focus on the paragraph which shows also the involvement of the operational commander in the area. I'm starting on: "On that occasion --" that occasion is the meeting with the operation group commander Colonel Mladen Fuzul. "On that occasion I pointed out the real causes of the situation which, at one point, developed into a state of anarchy. Namely, since this was a unit whose members were mostly from this area, most of them stayed in town drinking the entire night. Law and order were violated and various crimes were committed, after which the OG commander issued a strict order forbidding all HV members from entering the town of Benkovac. He - and in my understanding that the OG Commander Fuzul, Colonel Fuzul - also summonsed the leadership of Benkovac municipality and the chief of the PU, police administration, to point out the omissions of both sides. At the meeting we - and I understand by that - Colonel Fuzul - the military police, and civilian police agreed on how to eradicate such incidents and established, i.e., I proposed measures." That is just one example of several reports on the situation in Benkovac, situation that develops upon the arrival of elements the HV operating under the command of General Gotovina in Benkovac between the 6th and the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So they were drinking?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to have more information, I can also point you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I mean, you're comparing, there is no report in there about the unit went in there and burned down Benkovac, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But if the an officer of the military police states that the real cause of the situation which at one point developed into a state of anarchy, I assume he is referring to more than a few individuals having a beer or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is you're assumption the is what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I call it assumption or conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll call it an assumption. Thank you. Now, let's get back to how we veered off on this topic, which is again fundamentally you and I agree is that your report made no effort to distinguish between HVO and HV, and I'm glad we agree on that. HVO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do. If do you not, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it should be rather more precisely. I didn't make a distinction between the forces that were subordinated to General Gotovina at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You cited a document now, a 65 ter. Before we move on I do want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it was 65 ter 5658 which is still open, and I would have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually he said 65 ter 2741.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can check the number. I don't know whether it helps to give you the ERN?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay. Okay. I will move on. There is some confusion on my part here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is footnote 1325 in the second part of the report, and I will check whether have I the right 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It's actually a different document that I will be referring to later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Getting back to this issue of -- you now acknowledge you didn't make a distinction between the forces that were subordinated to General Gotovina at that moment in time. Would you agree with me that the HVO was subordinated to General Gotovina, but was, in fact, a military that was part of a different country without getting into the legalities now of how we would argue this, but it was subordinated to General Gotovina pursuant to an agreement between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces that were included in OG North were subordinated to General Gotovina based on, yeah, probably agreement or an order. I'm not sure -- you mean, I can make a leap to the Split agreement, but I assume there would be more specific agreement even though I haven't seen them. But I understand that what pointing at with the agreement between Mr. Izetbegovic and Tudjman, i.e., the Split agreement of 22nd July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question hypothetically: In NATO, the forces of one country could be operationally subordinated to the commander of a different country, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And there would be particular subordination. Relationships will be established for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Now the operational commander from that other country doesn't typically discipline the forces of the army of the other country that is subordinated to him, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I think it is important in that context to make a distinction between the subordination relationships that exist in NATO and those that exist been the HV and the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's make those distinctions. Is it your position that the Code of Military Discipline of the HV gave commanders the powers to discipline members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting with the basics, I believe -- I consider Article 26 of the Code of Discipline very relevant in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, please. Is the HVO part of the HV in the Code of Military Discipline?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then Article 26 does not apply to forces that are not part -- that are not the HV, does it? Let me put it a different way. If the United States army subordinated itself to General Gotovina in Bosnia in the fall of 1995, General Gotovina couldn't say, Well, under Article 26 of my Code of Military Discipline, I can discipline members of the US army, could he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think -- I mean you cannot compare the relationship between the HV and the HVO, which did not, by the way date from the Split agreement but dated from such earlier, with a kind of hypothetical scenario where US forces would be subordinated to the HV in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in that context we have discussed documents like, for example, D656 where General Gotovina appoints an HVO officer as the commander of the town of Drvar in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is hard to image that General Gotovina has no authority over the HVO, whereas at the same time he is issuing very strict orders as to how order and discipline has to be maintained in areas where the HVO is operating under his command. We also have the order for the -- the curfew in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, cite me one disciplinary measure taken by General Gotovina against a member of the HVO, and I mean disciplinary measures defined by the Code of Military Discipline or disciplinary sentences. Let me talk about minor and major violations, both. Give me one.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is obviously a distinction between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, would you please first answer the question whether you are able to give such an example. If you wanted to add anything to that, we will hear from you after the direct answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no example on the imposition of disciplinary measures by General Gotovina against members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have an example of any HV officer issuing a disciplinary measure pursuant to the HV Code of Military Discipline against a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would to have check, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you see in the monthly or quarterly reports prepared by the Split Military District or any other Military District, when they break it down according to unit in terms of measures taken, that the HVO was included for reporting purposes in reports of disciplinary measures that were being taken?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there any document that you can cite me to, putting aside your military experience, education, et cetera, any document that you can point me to, to support your conclusion that General Gotovina could issue disciplinary measures and/or sentences against members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if General Gotovina can issue an order to appoint a town commander with clearly defined responsibilities in the area of discipline and military justice or the prevention of crimes for the town of Drvar and that is D656, and if he can decree or impose a military curfew in the town of Jajce in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if he has no powers to enforce these orders or at least there are people who violate that order, to have the procedures started, i.e., send reports to the appropriate authorities in the HVO, these orders do not make much sense. So I agree with you that it was most likely again from the material that I reviewed, it is not -- General Gotovina did not impose the disciplinary sentences -- measures or sentences to members of the HVO, but at least he was in a position to discover violations and report them to the appropriate authorities in the HVO. And that applies also to the subordinate officers, I mean commanding officers of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Theunens, your report cites the fact that it's the SIS HVO the SIS -- I mean the HVO military police, et cetera, that is, in fact, reporting these measures to Mostar, right? You wouldn't know about there stuff if it wasn't being reported.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not entirely correct because the orders -- I mean the two orders I referred to by General Gotovina, the town commander and the curfew, General Gotovina would not issue such orders if he didn't see a requirement to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But let's talk about this right now. Are -- do you understand the difference in General Gotovina's role as an occupation commander in Bosnia and as a commander in his home country who turned over matters to the civilian government on the 6th of August, 1995? Do you as a military expert acknowledge a difference -- a different obligation that a commander would have when he is occupying territory and when he is a -- in effect, in peacetime in his home territory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a distinction may be relevant for maybe legal discussions as to whether what was the authority of General Gotovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as pointed you out a different country or not, but from the point of view of enforcement of military discipline, in my view, there is no drinks between the two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, it is it not just -- it's not just a distinction for legal discussion. You, at page 314, subparagraph S, you reach the following conclusion. You say: "Based on the documents reviewed for the preparation of this report, it appears that only in after the launching of Operation Maestral, Colonel General Ante Gotovina takes more vigorous action to prevent or punish crimes. On 17 September 1995, Gotovina appoints a military town commander in Drvar, BiH, to protect the town from looting and destruction as the area is designated for the settling of displaced Croats. On 22 September 1995, General Gotovina imposes a military curfew in Jajce and so on." That is it your opinion in your conclusion. Isn't it essential in reaching that conclusion that you first understand the authority of a commander as an occupying commander versus the authority of a commander where constitutional law has been restored in his area in his home country?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered the question. I do not see a reason to make a distinction when we are referring to the imposition or the enforcement of military discipline among subordinate forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So it's your view when you say that paragraph that only in active and launching of Operation Maestral does he take more vigorous action. That it is your conclusion, for example, that on the 10th of August he could have imposed a town commander to control Benkovac, let's say?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, from what I read out of -- what I considered 65 ter 2714, in any event, English page 328, part 2 of my report, we can see there that the operational commander, General Fuzul, he calls the civilian authorities to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 6th or the 7th August, because the report by Grncaric is dated 8th of August. And there we see that the operational commander, based on the report of Grncaric, called the military police commander the chief of the civilian police or the representative of the civilian police, as well as -- it is described as the leadership of the Benkovac municipality. In my view, those are the civilian authorities. And based again on the report of Grncaric, the operational commander tries to coordinate the whole matter and tries to solve the situation. He seems to take -- he is taking the lead in this area at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And again my question is: So it's your position as of the 10th of August onward, General Gotovina could name a town commander to control Benkovac like did he in Drvar in late September 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am not stating that he could, for example, impose a town commander. It is obvious that there should have been for such a decision there needs to be coordination with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses between the questions and answers. It is becoming impossible for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to the interpreters and to the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The point is this: Would you agree with me that if General Gotovina after the proclamation that the constitution order had been restored in Croatia on the 7th of August, after that point in time, if General Gotovina imposes a town commander or a military curfew on the territory of the Split Military District, without permission from the civilian government and or President Tudjman, he has executed effectively a coup d'etat?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the way how you word it now it is it clear that the -- that would not be regular. What I was trying to explain before the interruption was that the military structures based on the documents I have seen, i.e., the forces under command of General Gotovina, are best organised structures in the area at that moment in time that. That is one aspect. The second aspect is it there are problems with the enforcement of law and order. Now, one would expect that the military commander, i.e., General Gotovina, based on his own observations as well the reporting he has received from subordinate commanders SIS political affairs and the military police would inform his superior, that, well, maybe it is it too early to hand over power to the civilian authorities, or maybe we should establish mechanisms in order to provide assistance to the civilian police and the civilian authorities in order maintain or restore law and order in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your suggestion that General Gotovina should suggest to his superiors the suspension of constitutional law and the imposition of military law in the area. That's what he failed to do.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry for the transcript. That is not what I was proposing or what I was stating. How -- General Gotovina can inform his superiors about the problems he has. I would expect that as a military commander, he wants to have the largest degree as possible over his forces and over his zone of responsibility, because as we see from the documents, the fighting is not over on the 10th of August. And that then based on the -- on the constitution and the -- and the legislation of the Republic of Croatia, a solution is developed involving the civilian authorities at the highest level as well as military authorities in order to allow the commander on the ground to indeed control the situation in his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if now is a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a suitable time for the break. We will have a break and resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, during the break were you able to find any reference in the -- operational diary to burning and looting by HV on the territory of the Republic of Croatia after the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- not in the operational diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before we get into -- back to the topic of the HVO, let me show you one additional document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I forgot to tender into evidence 65 ter 5658, if I could do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D989 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 4609, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report sent by the Split Military District to the Main Staff on the 29th of August. And it is a report of a survey of military infrastructure facilities that are being -- in addition to facilities, it talks about those being guarded by HV. For example, if we go to page 4, there's a subsection, facilities that the HV used and guarded before the Storm operation and is still using and guarding it. Go two pages in. Now, this is a report by General Gotovina, and in it he says, he is talking about transferring authorities of these to the civilian authorities and he says: "In the case of 31 facilities that are on our list, it is necessary, according to our statements to assign around 900 people to carry out guard duties. Engagement of the Split Military District units at the front line from Martin Brod to M. Ticevo and the execution of the demobilization order will make guarding of so many important military facilities even more complicated. In our opinion it is very important to solve the question of future needs of the Split MD ZP units, and in accordance with that, solve the question of allotment of facilities and question of their guarding and maintenance." Now, would you agree with me that the demobilization -- Let me rephrase that. General Gotovina points to the fact that he still has a front line in Bosnia that he is maintaining, Martin Brod to Ticevo, and he is guarding facilities, military facilities, and he says the execution of the demobilization order will make guarding of these facilities even more complicated. Would you agree with me that the demobilization that was in progress at that time imposed certain hardships on the Split Military District Command given its ongoing responsibilities for combat in Bosnia, which was about to take place and its guarding of facilities in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit number D990 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, some of the documents you looked at, Mr. Theunens, particularly in the fall of 1995, have in the heading section as to who is issuing the reports or orders, it says "Croatian forces" instead of Split MD command. Are you familiar with some of those documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I want to discuss them, I assume that will you show them, but I have no particular recollection of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you -- are you familiar with the fact that General Gotovina was using the title Commander of Croatian Forces in the fall of 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the specific documents again. It is probably the case, but it is helpful if you're going to discuss a specific document that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you one.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I mean, the one where he appoints --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you one document, 65 ter 5545, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Just for the sake of completeness, D656 where he appoints the town commander in Drvar used the heading "Split Military District Command, Vrba Forward Command Post." There's a similar one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let look at the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The upper left-hand corner says: "The Croatian Forces." In Croatian, "Hrvatske Snage."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is an operational formation; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The author of the document must have had reason to use Croatian forces. It would indicate that -- and I don't want to go too far in drawing the wrong conclusion, but it would indicate that there is no distinction made between HV and HVO. I mean, on the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, would it indicate that there's a coalition force between the HV and the HVO, which the coalition is being referred to as Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. Whereby, at least from the military point of view, the expression coalition should be defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is a coalition force?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as I have not seen a document defining what the coalition means, i.e., who is the commander, what is his authority, what are the composing elements, then it is impossible for me to draw a conclusion by what is meant by a coalition force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you haven't seen a document defining what the coalition means, who is the commander, what is his authority, what are the composing elements, with respect to the HV and HVO, then what were you able to draw the conclusion -- upon what were you aware you drawing the conclusion that General Gotovina could issue disciplinary measures to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have not used the expression "coalition" in my report. I didn't specifically use the expression "Croatian forces." Secondly, the fact -- and I apologise for repeating myself, but the fact that General Gotovina issues an order to appoint a town commander in Drvar, and he does that under the heading "Split Military District Command Vrba Forward Command Post," that's D656, there's also the order for the transfer of a platoon of the 72nd Military Police Battalion to Drvar on the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to get to ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But to answer the question, if General Gotovina issues all these orders, it means he has the authority to do so, otherwise it would have stopped after the first order and he would not issue such orders anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order needs to result in certain effects. It is not -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if, again let's go hypothetical. If the US army imposes military law on a city in Iraq, does that mean that they have disciplinary authority over British forces in Iraq?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand the question, even though I would like to have it clarified because I would first need to know what is the relation between the British forces and the US forces in the city where the US army imposes military law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you asked the witness whether he was familiar with the fact that General Gotovina was using the title Commander of Croatian Forces. This -- then later on, the coalition forces were introduced as a term. Now, the only thing I really heard the witness say until now is that he doesn't have the details of forces that may have been under a Joint Command or not. Let's try to find out not on the basis of hypothetical matters, but please put the question to Mr. Theunens which brings us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, but his answer it precisely where I would like to get to. Because I would like to know -- when talking about different forces, you say, Well, I need to know -- just the fact that one country's forces are controlling a town, you can't tell what the relationship is with the other country's force because you say, first you would first need to know what is the relation between the British forces and US forces in the city where the US army imposes military law. So now going back to the HV/HVO, you keep going back to Drvar and Jajce. Let me ask you, using your own methodology, first let's look at what is the relationship and the agreement between the HV and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I explain -- I'm sorry. Do you mean the relation during Operation Maestral?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I mean from the Split Agreement until the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I will start with Maestral, but if you want we can go page by page from the relevant sections in my report, but from Maestral, as it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I gave you the time-frame because I don't think there is any difference between Maestral, Storm, summer 1995, Southern Sweep, the starting point that I'm giving you is from the Split agreement on the 23rd of July, 1995, until the Dayton Agreement, what is the relationship, and using your phrase again, you need -- you first need to know what is the relation between the forces. So what is the relation between the HV and the HVO between the time-period I just gave you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will start with Operation Maestral where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, a specific question is put to you, starting 23rd July 1995, whether that is -- whatever operation that is. But you could tell us perhaps whether that date is in the course of what operation so that we would then know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 22nd of July refers to the conclusion of the Split agreement between President Izetbegovic, President Tudjman, and the president of the so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and this agreement among other things allows for the presence of Croatian forces, i.e., HV forces of the Republic or Croatia on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also for the Bosniak authorities to ask Croatia for military assistance. I'm summarizing the agreement. Two days later Operation Ljeto is launched under the command of General Gotovina, whereby General Gotovina is in command of forces belonging to the HV, i.e., Split Military District, including 7th Guards Brigade and the 1st Croatian Guard, as well as forces of the HVO, and all these forces operate under the command of General Gotovina. During Operation Storm, elements of the HVO continued to participate in the operations on the -- call it the HV side, under the command of General Gotovina, and we see the same situation during Operation Maestral, as well as Juzni Potez in October 1995. Maestral was in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in all those operations, what is the -- again going back to your question, what is the nature of the relationship between the HV and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the HVO that are participating in these operations are subordinated to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But again I'm talking it -- trying to ask you the question, because you have raised the issue of what is the definition of coalition. Because you said you didn't see how it was defined, et cetera. What is -- when you subordinated to General Gotovina, you mean operationally subordinated, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the beginning of my testimony, I explained that, for example, in NATO there are specific subordination relations -- relationships that are applied in different situations. Without going into detail, one of these concept is the concept of the combined joint task force, whereby, for example, in the case of KFOR, there is an American or an Italian or a German Force Commander, whereby for each and every troop-contributing nation there are agreements established as to what the authority is over the Force Commander over these national forces that are part of the combined joint task force. In general, countries do not give -- hand over disciplinary authority. However, there will be a force provost marshall, i.e., a force, military police force, which has the authority to investigate alleged violations of discipline or even military justice committed by members of the national contingents whereby depending on the specific situation, but in general, the results of the investigation will be handed over to a national contingent commander who is then expected to take the appropriate measures. Again I'm talking about in general because these agreements, they can be an encyclopedia of hundreds of pages. I know that for the HV/HVO no such specific subordination relations existed, i.e., I haven't seen any document limiting the authority of General Gotovina over the HVO forces that were subordinated to him during Ljeto, Storm, Maestral, and Juzni Potez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Interesting conclusion at the end, Mr. Theunens. Because as you were talking about NATO, the disciplinary authority of the other country's commander only comes if the agreement of the first country -- with the agreement of the first country, right? You don't say in NATO every commander, unless there is an agreement otherwise, an operational commander can discipline the troops of another country, right? In other words, you are talking about in the NATO context, agreements on -- you say in general countries do not hand over disciplinary authority. And then -- and then, right? That's the first point.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the concept of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, hold on now. Now, they can hand it over if they reach a specific agreement with that country to allow disciplinary authority by the other country's commander, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I have not seen such an agreement and again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise to the court reporter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue seems to be, but correct me if I'm wrong, that if there is agreement in which disciplinary powers are transferred, then the situation is clear. If there is no agreement, then you would have to consider whether it is remained with the command under which those forces usually operate, or whether it, as a consequence of subordination, is moved to the operative command under which that unit is operating. That seems to be the issue. Now, Mr. Theunens explained to us that, at least that's how I understood your testimony, that you're not aware of subordination under a foreign command without any specific agreement; that's clear. Now apparently Mr. Theunens says that he is not aware of any specific agreement here between HVO and HV, and apparently you, Mr. Misetic, and, Mr. Theunens, disagree on what the consequences of that situation are. That seems to be the issue if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure we disagree when it comes to what happens in NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. I don't understand how he got from the conclusion where he says countries reach agreements on subordination. Countries reach agreements on these disciplinary provosts, I believe he said.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Force Provost Marshall, which is the NATO slang for the -- I mean, it existed also in UNPROFOR. There was a Force Provost Marshall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which by agreement then has the subordinated troops subject to discipline of the Force Provost Marshall, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They will investigate the matters, but they can -- -- excuse me, they will investigate the matter, and again it -- you really have to look at the specific agreement, but in general they will investigate violations of discipline or justice, and then hand over the matter to national authorities, whereby, of course, it is expected that the national authorities, i.e., the authorities of the country to which the perpetrator of the violation of military discipline or military justice belongs. That these authorities will take the appropriate measures, and because, just to finalise, I know examples of UNPF, for example, that the Force Commander can send members of the force home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My -- this very specific issue for me is this: I agree with you that, at least I think agree with you, that, for example, this Force Provost Marshall is by agreement given the ability to investigate the matter which is fine, then you go and say you haven't found any agreements between HV/HVO, and therefore, your conclusion is there were no agreements limiting General Gotovina's disciplinary power over the HVO, as if without agreements General Gotovina has that power, whereas in the into the context, I think you're saying absent agreement the commander of the -- the operational commander doesn't have that power. So I'm wondering why in the NATO context you -- I agree with you, say operational commanders absent agreement don't have disciplinary authority, but when you talk about General Gotovina you say he as an operational commander has that authority absent agreement otherwise.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the answer is short. It's a different situation. When reviewing Croatian military doctrine, I haven't seen any reference to the specific command and control relations that exist within NATO armies, even in the national context. If I as a battalion commander of a armoured battalion receive an infantry company under my command, it can be operational command, tactical command, it can be under control. That -- the arrangement that is made and even if is from the same country, can have an impact on my disciplinary authority. As I mentioned Croatian doctrine I have not seen any such restrictions. I haven't seen it in the Code of Discipline, and when we look at the practical implementation during Ljeto, Storm, Maestral, and Juzni Potez, I see indeed that, for example, in his book, P482, General Gotovina states -- I mean that all forces operated under the commander -- under the command of the command for the Croatian forces, whereby for military documents I have reviewed, well, the commander of all forces conducting these operations in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District for what Storm is concerned by Ljeto, Maestral, Juzni Potez, the overall commander for these operations is General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, we seem to go off an end up someplace that I'm not sure answers my question. You say you haven't seen any agreement that would subordinate the HVO for disciplinary purposes to the commander of the Split Military District. You have already testified you see no examples of any discipline ever being meted out by any HV commander to a member of the HVO, right? And yet you then talk about Croatian doctrine -- and let me just put to you: The HV commanders had no disciplinary authority over members of the HVO, and you haven't found any document to support any conclusion to the contrary, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
