utterances.text: No. Because the documents I have seen, for example, to appoint a town commander in Drvar to send or to order a platoon of the 72nd Military Police Battalion to monitor an access road to Drvar to impose a curfew in Jajce, if General Gotovina had no disciplinary authority over the HVO, he would issue such an order to an HVO commander, instead of issuing such an order to all the forces. At least from the military point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I understand what keeps you apart. Mr. Misetic, you very much emphasise that under NATO that without an explicit consent or agreement, disciplinary powers would not be with the commander to which the units, which are usually are not under his command, are subordinated. I understand Mr. Theunens's testimony, but he will certainly correct me if I'm wrong. That a situation where no specific regulations are made for disciplinary command is as they say in latin casus non dabilis, a case which doesn't exist because there always is a specific arrangements. Which leads to the next question, Mr. Theunens, would you be in a position if this hypothetical situation that in NATO, if there would be no specific regulation for the disciplinary powers, would you be able to answer with whom the disciplinary powers would be once a unit is subordinated to a -- to say a foreign command? Or is it so hypothetical that you say well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not in a -- it is very hypothetical, but military logic that would that be it would be the highest national member in that multi-national force, i.e., national means members of the same country as the alleged violators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say if there is no specific regulation, disciplinary powers would be within the command of all units of subordinated, whether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, excuse me, Mr. President. What I'm saying is that in the hypothetical case that is there no agreement, then of course the -- the call it the multi-national commander he can discover or even report a violation, but he will have to send it to the highest national representative of the alleged country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so reporting by the highest commanders, but finally to deal with the by the national commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now we move away from NATO. We find ourselves, as I understand, in a situation where no specific regulations exist. Mr. Misetic asks you what's the basis for your conclusions you present, that the highest command to which the -- and that's now become specific, the HVO units were subordinated, what role and why that highest command which you said was General Gotovina, what his role was in disciplinary matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the documents I have seen, and I refer for that to -- for Ljeto to the entries in the operational diary for Maestral what is included in second part of my report, for example page 370, General Gotovina at least has the authority to task his military police to report all violations to him. The same applies to the town commander he appoints. Now, I have not seen any documents indicating that General Gotovina takes disciplinary measures against members of the HVO, and I have not seen documents indicating that, for example, the prosecutor at the military disciplinary court in Split takes or decides about sentences against members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does that mean because that apparently is the question when it didn't happen that there was no authority to do so, or do you say, I don't know, or what's -- what's your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, and I'm just quoting from a document in P71 the operational diary, we see -- or we may remember the entry where it is said that shoot in the legs of all members of the -- of the armed forces who loot, I'm paraphrasing a bit, but we can find reference back. And there's no distinction made between members of the HV or the HVO. Now there is no Code of Discipline that says people who commit violations of military discipline or even who commit crimes should be shot in the legs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do take it, but do you understand this to be do everything can you do to prevent looting or further looting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours, and there is no distinction made between members of the HV or members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But the way in which I phrased it, I said: "Do everything can you do," the issue is what can you do apparently or what you are competent to do, not to say to your next door neighbour, don't loot, but if he continues, what action to be taken? Could I ask you one very factual question. Are you aware of disciplinary measures or disciplinary sentences imposed on HVO servicemen when they were subordinated to General Gotovina, because you have already told us that you have no examples of disciplinary measures or disciplinary sentences imposed upon them by the HV command, by General Gotovina. Now any other command you are aware of that ever imposed disciplinary measures to these HVO service members when they were subordinated to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and I will check my report again tomorrow morning, but based on the knowledge I have now, I am not aware of such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So either they never committed any disciplinary violations, or there was a vacuum or -- we'll see. I'm asking you whether you could give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I mean -- another option would be that we don't have the document, even though maybe measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You didn't make it part of your task to review all the archives of the HVO as well for this report, did you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I did, for example, searches like "Gotovina" as the search term within 30 discipline, and then discipline with a star, for example. That is how the database functions, and it would not make a distinction between the origin of the document, whether it would be HV, HVO, or another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Following up where we got to this point. The highest national force commander, if we were to use that terminology, of the HVO within the Croatian forces was General Blaskic, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly at the time of Ljeto. I'm not sure for Maestral and Juzni Potez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To check on what disciplinary measures General Blaskic may have taken, you would have to do a search in your database that says "Blaskic within 30 of discipline," right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example. Or I could also do a search Gotovina within, for example, 30 HVO, because it may well be, and that brings us back to Article 26. And I'm just trying to explain the practical importance of the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here for a second. When you ever Gotovina in your search, you miss all the disciplinary measures and sentences in which Gotovina is not involved or not within 30 words of that; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, of course when it comes to discipline, I also used other criteria. One of the things I was interested in was disciplinary measures imposed by General Gotovina, for example. And then that search criteria would be relevant, but of course in relation to the issue of discipline, I did many more searches using other key words, not just restricting me to the name of Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you don't recall doing a specific subsearch for Blaskic and discipline or HVO and discipline, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic and discipline, I don't remember. HVO and discipline, I think I did. I don't recall exactly whether I focussed on a specific unit, but certainly in the context of Ljeto, I did so. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Ljeto is prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But from the documents I have reviewed, I have not seen any indication that there was a different command and control arrangement between the forces of the HV and the HVO that were -- that participated or that conducted these operations under the command of General Gotovina. And if you allow me, I would like to give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even under the same arrangements, the facts could have been different, isn't it? I asked you whether you searched for disciplinary measures or sentences imposed on HVO members. Now you said I'm not aware of it. You didn't find any of them under -- in relation to Gotovina, you didn't find any of them in relation to HVO commanders, which means that even if the arrangements were the same, it could be that examples could be found under the same arrangement, but in a different time-frame, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and that is why the aspect of time -- I would have to check again which search terms I exactly used, because there are hundreds of terms and I haven't saved all of them, but it is true that sometimes I imposed also time limitations because just for the facility of the searches. If you allow me, I would like to give a brief practical explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I allow Mr. Misetic to put the next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, looking at the document on the screen, you will note the security situation upon the entry of the Croatian forces into Mrkonjic Grad. It says: "Not a single case of arson has been registered." I'm interested in the second paragraph. It says: "The livestock is a huge problem. The animals wander through the town and the neighbouring villages. A certain number of animals are still in the stables, and they have to be collected in the coming several days, since there is a possibility that they will die." Now, in a situation where a force takes over an area where forces and people have left and livestock is left behind with no one to tend to it, what should a military do in that situation concerning that livestock?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Procedures for the dealing with livestock should be included in the order for attack. For example, the logistics service -- and I will phrase it, logistic service, they will have specific assets available. There will also be veterinarians within the attacking force in order to take care of these issues because that animals will be a huge problem as they can create diseases. That is also why, for example, killed soldiers will have to be evacuated as soon as possible and buried as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I interrupt you here. Apparently Mr. Misetic asked you what should be done, which is a matter of substance, take them away, kill them, whatever. Your answer, however, is about procedure. Now, both may be relevant, but I'd like to make a clear distinction between the two. You said you should regulate it. Where Mr. Misetic asked you what you a regulation or at least what action should look like. So could we distinguish between procedure and substance. You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. Substance follows from the procedure so there should be -- I mean, the animals should be secured. Measures should be taken to prevent them from wandering around the battlefield, so lock them up in stables or facilities where they can be kept under control. If you're in a position to feed them, then you feed them. If you can't feed them well, you find other solutions, but you avoid that they are killed at random because then corpses will stay where they have been killed, and there is a risk of disease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this they starve at random because there is no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then you make arrangements to have them buried as soon as possible in a way that prevents -- again, that diseases can spread. That is one of the problems at least in the military that dead bodies that are spread on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That goes without saying. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May this document be marked and tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D991 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'd like to take you to first to page 315 of your report, paragraph W. And there you conclude: "Based on the documents that have been reviewed for the preparation of this report, Gotovina and his subordinate commanders only enforce the military discipline system when the violations or breaches or crimes directly affect the combat readiness and/or operations of the Split Military District or the immediate interest of Croatia, i.e., relations with UNCRO?" And now I'd like to take you to page 160 of part 1 of your report. And there at paragraph D, in talking about the Croatian system you say: "Military discipline refers to the exact full and timely conduct of military service." And what I'd like you to explain is what is the difference between General Gotovina's understanding of military discipline, which you described at page 315, paragraph W, and your understanding of it, in the Croatian system, which is described at page 160, paragraph D.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference I see, Your Honours, is that based on the review of the documents included in my report, I conclude that General Gotovina has a rather narrow interpretation of the concept of military discipline, i.e., he sees military discipline exclusively focussed on the accomplishment of the specific combat tasks and combat operations. So, for example, if a soldier fails to present himself in time at the morning assembly, disciplinary measures maybe taken in that case. He also reacts very swiftly when there is a problem with UNCRO. Example, the incidents between the commander of the Split garrison and UNCRO members at an UNCRO check-point on the -- on the 4th of August, General Gotovina almost immediately orders to arrest the commander of the Split garrison. In other cases, and I refer now to the incidents of looting and burning that are reported during and after Operation Storm, the fact that they continued to be reported and that at the same time orders are issued at a high rate, indicates to me that there is no -- or not the same willingness as there is in the -- to earlier situations I described to act against violations of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's first get to the first part where you say it's a narrow interpretation. You say: "He sees military discipline exclusively focussed on the accomplishment of the specific combat tasks and combat operations." First of all, if you reviewed the 1300-plus disciplinary measures taken into the third quarter, you would have found that all of those disciplinary measures were not related exclusively to failure in combat operations, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can I only conclude on the material I have reviewed and that starts on page 381. For example, on page 384 I list the various breaches and violations of military discipline, which one can find in the reporting of the Split Military District Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But so from your answer, then, I take it that you didn't review what all the 1300 disciplinary measures were, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't remember the exact number of -- what I reviewed, whether it was 1300 or less. I believe there were less. So if you have examples, I mean, of other violations and breaches, of course, I am available to review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you're the one who is given the conclusion that he only issues disciplinary measures when they're related to combat tasks. So I'm asking you, did you review all the disciplinary measures first before arriving at a conclusion as to what he only imposes discipline for?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude that he issued disciplinary measures or had disciplinary proceedings started or launched in other cases, but the majority, I mean, the overwhelming majority of the measures I have seen deal with matters that are almost exclusively focussed on -- combat readiness and the execution of combat tasks and operations. In a very narrow sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you at page 160 say: "Military discipline refers to the exact full and timely conduct of military service." What is the distinction between General Gotovina's -- in your view, General Gotovina's interpretation and your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distinction based on the reports is that General Gotovina's interpretation focuses exclusively on combat aspects, i.e., that the forces achieve the mission within the imposed time-frame, with a minimum of losses, almost -- I don't like to use the express at any cost, but from the documents I reviewed, it seems that the manner in which they accomplished the mission, as long as friendly losses are minimal and the goals or the objectives are reached within the imposed time-frame, then the mission is accomplished. Whereas, the regulations also include elements like limitation of collateral or undesired damaged during the execution of the mission and also afterwards, i.e., military discipline also applies to the fact that armed forces should not loot or -- members of armed forces should not loot or burn or kill animals during the execution of the task as well as afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we've already covered the relationship between the criminal law and the disciplinary law, so I won't go back into that with you now. Mr. Theunens, let me ask you this: What are a -- an occupation -- occupying commander's -- well, let me take it back. Generally speaking, are you familiar with what an occupation commander's responsibilities are under international law in occupying territory of a foreign country?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert, so I'm not familiar with the details of the international law in relation to the authority of the -- of a commander or the responsibility of a commander under the occupational regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you think that General Gotovina as an occupational commander in western Bosnia in the fall of 1995, unlike yourself, would have been or should have been familiar with his international obligations as an occupying commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he should at least have been familiar with his obligations as a military commander as such. And if the fact that he is an occupational commander in -- what you describe as a foreign country, includes additional obligations I would expect him to be also familiar with those obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, is there any dispute that Bosnia was a foreign country at that time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that. But even before the signing of the Split agreement, forces of the HV were operating on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, so what? I mean, his duties as an occupational commander -- well, let me -- let me ask it a different way. In evaluating -- and you have evaluated General Gotovina in your report in western Bosnia in 1995, do you think that if, in fact, General Gotovina was issuing orders pursuant to his duties as an occupational commander, it should have been incumbent upon you to learn what the obligations of an occupation commander are before evaluating General Gotovina's actions in western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders I have reviewed, orders by General Gotovina, do not make reference to a status that you have introduced of occupational commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the orders don't need to make reference to it. Whether they make reference to it or not doesn't change the fact that he is an occupying commander in western Bosnia in the fall of 1995. Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I mean, the documents I have reviewed do not mention the term occupying commander or occupation commander, and I don't consider it of relevance, I mean this concept for the conclusions that I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know what the responsibilities of an occupation commander are, do you take into consideration that that might affect how you are looking at issues like appointing a town commander for Drvar, imposing a military curfew in Jajce. Do you think would be maybe useful for you to first find out what the duties of an occupational commander are?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that is relevant because when we look at D204 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what Mr. Misetic puts to you, if I understand him well, is the following: You relied several times on examples of the way in which General Gotovina exercised what you say, must have been his powers, because otherwise he couldn't have given that orders or could not have made those appointments. Now Mr. Misetic is asking you where you draw parallels from that system, whether this, as you testified, rather broad concept or at least broad exercise of these powers, whether the position of a commander whose troops occupy foreign territory might be a clue to understanding this situation, if I -- Mr. Misetic, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as to see whether the conclusions you have drawn from those examples to what you said would have been within his disciplinary powers of units which are subordinated to him, although not part of the regular forces he commands over, whether we have to adjust or to reconsider, or whether you would have to adjust or reconsider such conclusions, that is, I think, the relevance of what Mr. Misetic puts to. Now, although, I'm not under an obligation to explain to you the relevance. Perhaps it's good that you are aware of my understanding of the relevance of this question is. Could you please try to answer the question, whether you have -- whether you have explored the duties of a commander of an occupying force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not explored the duties of a commander of an occupying force in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, one moment, please. Let me put this to you. You've looked at a series of orders yesterday -- Friday and today from before Storm, during Storm, and after Operation Storm issued by General Gotovina, and we've established that you don't know of any reports after the 18th of August going to General Gotovina about a problem of burning and looting by units in the Split Military District on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. So let me put it to you this way: Concerning your opinion that the orders lacked effectiveness, if, in fact, as Mr. Flynn says the burning peaked at the 20th of August, if, in fact, there is no evidence of notice to General Gotovina or the Split Military District Command of reports of burning and looting after -- on the territory of the Republic of Croatia after the orders issued by the Split Military District Command on the 18th of August, and if, in fact, General Gotovina's orders particularly the order of the 10th of August, resulted in an increase of 151 per cent in the number of disciplinary measures being taken in the Split Military District in the third quarter of 1995, didn't those orders have effectiveness?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to D654, which is issued on the 31st of August. It is by the commander of OG West, but he refers to an order by General Gotovina, and the order starts: "Commander of Split Military District units in their zones of responsibility in newly liberated territory of the RH, Republic of Croatia, shall take all necessary measures to ensure that all military infrastructure facilities are placed under full supervision and protection." The next paragraph states: "Stop all devastation regardless of what the facility's purpose is (barracks, depot, training ground, residential building, and so forth)." The order continues then. "What I'm trying to say is that the fact that on the 31st of August, an order of a subordinate unit of the Split Military District when referring to what is described as the liberated territory of the RH shows that actually the problem or the problems that existed prior to the 18th of August, at least based on the fact that on the 31st an order dealing with similar issues is again issued, shows that these problems still exist. And whether they are less of them or more, that may be another matter. But the commander of OG West, and he refers to an order of General Gotovina, considers it important to repeat to his subordinates in an order that they should not devastate buildings, whatever the building may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Theunens, let me put to you I think we saw a document before where General Gotovina was talking about handing over buildings that were under military control to the civilian authorities. That was on the 29th, I believe. This is an order on the 31st. You don't know, or you have no information to know whether this is simply a reminder to everyone as the process of the handover takes place or whether there is any additional reports. As I said in my question, you didn't find any reports of any additional burnings or lootings by HV units, right? There are no reports? Political affairs, SIS, the Split Military District operational diary, right, after the 18th August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably correct. But orders are just not issued for reminding people or just issuing them again, I mean, for the sake of issuing them. An order is only issued if one expects it to be abided by. And in this case, if this is an reason, i.e., a problem which convinces the commander to issue the order. A commander who just issues orders well, when he feels like it, he will see that his authority will be undermined, because an order without measures to verify its implementation works counter-productive

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me put it a different way. Prior to that order on the screen, are you familiar between the 18th August and the date of this order, which is I believe is the 31st of August, any reports of burning of military facilities on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the Split Military District? Do you know of any reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question before. I said that the conclusion you draw is probably correct, but again the fact that there is no report does not necessarily mean it doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it doesn't necessarily mean that it did happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is as if I'm listening to two politicians. One emphasizing how much the situation has improved due to the diligent measures taken by the government, the other one stating that poverty is still not over yet, and that therefore, it was a failure. It is clear, and has been repeated several times that in the questions we find repeatedly reference made to no reports, increased number of disciplinary actions taken, et cetera, and in the answers we find again was the reporting complete, et cetera. I think the positions are relatively clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a point --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... end of my cross, and I wanted to put my case to him because it is his opinion, and later on you could say that I put it to their expert witness as to what our case is, and now I can thank Mr. Theunens for his time. Thank you, Mr. President for allowing me the time, and I concede the floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, Your Honour, it is probably best to have the break now so we can rearrange the furniture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be preferable. Could I get an estimate on the basis. I haven't asked Mr. Misetic before, and I am not in any way threatening you because I do understand that this is an important expert for you, and the Chamber has considered that it should perhaps be a bit less pushing to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you nevertheless give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was hoping Your Honour was going answer the question for me. I think about a week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hardly dare to address the third Defence team. Mr. Kuzmanovic I saw earlier on the transcript that I already allowed you to put a next questions to the witness, but, of course, I said Mr. Misetic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour it very much depends on the progress of Mr. Kay. But for this moment, I could predict a day, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will consider the estimates, and we'll first have a break. Mr. Theunens, I do not know whether are you free for Christmas, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No plans yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No plans yet. We'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the Chamber will closely follow how the cross-examination develops, and then we'll finally see to what extent we can meet your -- your needs. In order to avoid whatever misunderstanding when I made the reference to Christmas, it certainly was not to Orthodox Christmas. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, Mr. Kay is Defence counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, first of all, can I ask you what exactly you see your subject of expertise in these proceedings, if you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my subject of expertise is that I am familiar with command and control issues in the armed forces, as well as with aspects of the conflict in former Yugoslavia which are relevant in the context of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your expertise, the sources of information that you have primarily relied upon, if you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, do you mean the sources for this report or the sources on which I -- yeah, I base my knowledge and understanding of command and control on the one hand, and the conflict in the former Yugoslavia on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The sources for your role as an expert, what you have drawn upon to provide your report as evidence to the Court.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the report is based on mainly military documents originating from the HV, including documents by the HV Main Staff, Split Military District Command, Knin garrison command, as well as subordinate units and that applies specifically to the Split Military District Command, special police, as well as legislation and doctrinal manuals and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If there are documents that you have not seen in the preparation of this report that are material to the evidence that you have given, how would you view the provision of such material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would of course welcome any new documents that can assist me in -- in -- or any other documents that can assist me in assessing the conclusions or reviewing the conclusions I have drawn based on the material available to me, and if needed, amend these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try and proceed through this in a very orderly way, Mr. Theunens, but taking it subject by subject, and the first matter we'll deal with concerns the service rules, laws of the garrison that you refer to in your report that may bear some examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If, first of all we go to D32, Your Honours, with is the service regulations a document that the Court familiar with, and go to page 21 in the English where we have the section called: Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you have expressed in your report, Mr. Theunens, these were rules that were produced in 1992, and do you agree they were at a stage when the armed forces of the new Republic of Croatia were being structured?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the English first page to see in which month in 1992 they were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These were produced in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff of the HV was established in -- in, yeah, after September 1991, and I agree with you that at that stage the HV is still in very early stage of its development. As I have described in part 2 of the report also in 1992, 1993, 1994, the HV continues to develop. So whether in May 1992, they're still at earlier stage, it's difficult to conclude. One can state that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's probably enough of the answer for the moment.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because we will proceed through it. You've cited the regulations in your report, regulation 50. I'm turning to regulation 52, first of all, and to deal with what this regulation is about. And what it is about is the function of the garrison commander within the military system. Is that right, as a general heading?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it tells us what the garrison commander is responsible for. We see billeting, order, discipline, and service in the garrison. We see all units and institutions within the garrison being subordinate to the commander, as regards the issues of order, discipline, and service. And then in Rule 54, we see what the responsibilities of the garrison commander are, and they're to issue rules on order, discipline, and supervision of the behaviour of military persons in the garrison. No need to turn to page 22, which deals with other aspects, but we're looking at this issue of order and discipline primarily. Isn't that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the first paragraph of Article 54 states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the garrison commander is someone who, within an area in which the military has a -- a presence runs various facilities for the armed forces who may be part of that area, or who may be passing through the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to achieve order and discipline within a garrison, the garrison commander is entitled to issue various local rules by which those forces would have to comply with. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking an example. We have a garrison in a town. There is an old bridge, service vehicles cross that bridge. The garrison commander may put up an order saying that service vehicles must only cross that bridge at 30 kilometres per hour. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, there can be rules by the garrison commander relating to the married quarters where soldiers may live. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if they are outside of the barracks of the unit, I mean, the particular unit where these people live, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the English army it is known as "the patch." Is that an expression you know of?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard that expression yet, Your Honours, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the garrison commander may tell the wives of soldiers not to hang out their washing on Sundays or on Saturdays. That would be a local rule.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the case in the British Army, then I'm willing to believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to these rules that we are looking at here concerning the garrison, it is those matters within Regulation 52 that is the object of the regulation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say 52 and 54, but probably we mean the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm taking it in stages, as others are following.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in some bases there may be -- I don't know how familiar you are with garrisons. Perhaps if you can answer that question before I go on further.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for -- I mean, each military unit is part of a garrison. And like when I was stationed in Germany, our next operational command level was located 60 kilometres more to the east, but we were part of a garrison known as the Spich garrison, S-p-i-c-h, which was a smaller city south of Cologne. When I was part of the military intelligence and security service in Brussels, we were all, as officers, part of the Brussels garrison and, for example, that included that we could sit on court martials. There was a duty role for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The garrison, then, has within it this commander who provides those local rules which are the rules that others have to follow to enable there to be order and discipline of the military forces, whilst they are within the garrison. In summary, that is it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a correct summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To achieve that, of course, under Regulation 54, you have to issue those rules, which has as a precondition -- you know the place that you're serving at, that it is, in fact, a garrison in existence. That`s right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, but if it is not established whether or not the garrison exists, then it is hard to imagine there would be a commander. But, again, I'm not sure I understand the question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to Knin. Knin we know wasn't liberated by the Croatian forces until the 5th of August, 1995. And on that day, Mr. Cermak was appointed as a garrison commander for Knin. There had previously been someone appointed as an acting garrison commander, a Major Gojevic. But Major Gojevic was never sitting in Knin in that period before the 5th of August to enable him to draft any rules that may be necessary for order and discipline that may have to apply within Knin. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Major Gojevic was not sitting in Knin. D33 describes the municipalities that are covered by the Knin garrison, where it is put between --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're going to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to you take this in stages. We will cover every document. That's why I've said the time I have, and I want to make sure that you follow the argument in stages. I think it is better having observed matters over the last week. But be assured, I will be covering everything.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So indeed Major Gojevic was not sitting in Knin. I have not seen any orders or rules he established as the acting commander of the Knin garrison "pending its move" as is specified in D33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And in Regulation 52, when we look at it, it is correct that those rules that are the garrison rules are issued and thereby cause units and institutions within the garrison to be subordinate to those rules, because that is part of the system of running the garrison. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Taking our example of the road bridge with the speeding limit upon it, if a military truck from a unit not based in our garrison, we don't even have to think of Knin as I don't think there were such rules issued, but a truck from another military district area crossing that bridge would -- would have to respect that rule of the garrison put up by the commander.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Failure to do so, if a military policeman is standing at the other end of the bridge, he may stop the vehicle and thereafter take a number of steps, in relation to a disciplinary breach. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So even a member of the garrison command could do the same, if he sees the violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm taking the military police because that is a subject within this case, but someone else may also do that, and thereby be an enforcement of that rule on that particular soldier. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In according with the procedures established in the Code of Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving on now to the setting up of the garrisons, and we see at D33 a document that the Court is familiar with, dated the 16th of February, 1993, setting up of garrisons of the Croatian army, an order that was issued by the Chief of Staff, General Bobetko. And this, in 1993, as we know, set up the areas that were to be part of the particular garrisons, and we know at page 4 that this included Knin. Isn't that right? And if we just look at page 4.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it is in the document. It may be page 3. But any way, the Knin garrison is defined in this order of 16th February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: (E), Knin garrison, it's page 4 of the document that I have, but that doesn't matter. Who is ever on the control there, if we go to page 3. Page 2. Page 2. We'll see it. Because at this time in 1993, Knin garrison had been given an area, but it had not been established and subject to the jurisdiction and control of the Croatian armed forces as a geographical area. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We know that there is a body known as the Knin garrison operating in Gospic, but it is it not yet in Knin and obviously is not carrying out its duties in the actual Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will be looking at all those documents very soon. It says here: "Within the command of the Home Guard battalion of the Knin garrison." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the personnel for the Knin garrison is to provide it by a Home Guard Battalion that would normally be located in Knin but is -- consists of people originating from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn now to further documents within this exhibit that were annexed to it so that we can just cover a few details on the way. Turning to page 9 of the document that I have got, which is where this is a report on troop numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 5 on the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, that's the right document. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing this specific page which is on the left, but from other Split Military District documents, yeah, the figures on manpower are familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The sort of garrison headquarters you were talking about in Brussels, how many people worked in the garrison HQ?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection except -- no specific recollection except that in our system, normally that position would be a cumulative position, i.e., the first garrison I was part of, the garrison commander was actually the commander of the -- of the largest battalion in the area. And in Brussels, I believe it was the commander of the barracks where the -- the General Staff was located, but I'm not sure. And he may have had maximum one company available to him which was actually the headquarters company, i.e., a company which is tasked with the -- which is responsible for the functioning --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say "may," do you know?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an exact recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, best not put things in if you don't actually know, as it may cause further research. But we see there, the numbers certainly in the 31st of August, 1995, turning to the next page in the document, current status of unit being 10 people. If we turn to the next page, in September. The page after that, current status in unit, some eight people. And then if we could move to another document now. 65 ter 3514. This is a document dated the 28th of June, 1995. It's from the Split Military District Command, sent to General Gotovina, and it concerns numerical strength. And the document, first of all, if you look at the first page, is this a document that have you seen before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it, and I believe that it is included in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it is actually at the bottom of the page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There we are. The establishment should have nine people, but on the 28th of June, 1995, that third column, current number, shows three. So a few weeks before Operation Storm and the entry into Knin, it was a unit of three people. Is that a fact that you have considered in the production of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on now to D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can the last document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D992 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document is the organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison HQs, dated the 27th of August, 1993. And at that time in August 1993, it says, on the first page: "Garrison headquarters have not all been set up yet. They've not assumed their functions, and their locations, personnel recruitment, and prescribed tasks have not been assigned." The next paragraph refers to the desire to a comprehensive system in place and working so that command, cooperation, control at the level of garrison headquarters can take place and ensure comprehensive work order and discipline. If we turn to page 2 of the English. And just pausing here before we look at rule number 2, would you agree that on the 6th of August, 1995, the Knin garrison was not established as a working and functioning part of the Split Military District, to enable it to take on its role within the system. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there are two components in the question. First, the aspect of the 6th of August. I can only answer that already on the 5th, General Cermak issues an order. Now to what extent the Knin Military District is established -- excuse me, the Knin garrison, I apologise, the Knin garrison is established as a functioning garrison, I cannot conclude from the documents I reviewed. I can only say that General Cermak issues an order which is known as P506.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will be looking at that. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the second part is that the Knin garrison, as a working and functioning part of the Split Military District, without wanting to jump already now, I include in my report, English page 258, a section on the relations between the commander of the Knin garrison, General Cermak, and the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina, and that's in part 2 of the report, I should have said, whereby I state that the relation between the two of them is not as clear-cut as one would expect from military discipline. And again I just mention that here because I wasn't sure that I understood the question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will just tell you -- on the 6th of August, when the doors open at the garrison HQ in Knin, from the documents that have you seen, do you agree or disagree with the proposition that this was not functioning part of the Split Military District. As simple as that. We know the history of the matter. They go into Knin. The doors open. Are we looking at a well-oiled machine, or are we looking at something that is not established?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, Your Honours, based on the documents that I have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a look at some you have reviewed and some maybe you haven't reviewed. Looking at rule number 2 here, as you know, the garrison headquarters commands don't have an operational function, and the next part of the English. "... and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units, accept precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order, and discipline at the garrison headquarters, et cetera." And that is referring to those rules that I was mentioning right at the start of my questioning of you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't repeat it because I'm sure the Court has the point. And there are other tasks that are set out in number 3, requiring to establish cooperation and coordination with various bodies of a civil nature, as well as military, Ministry of Defence nature; and in four concrete tasks requiring to be set out regarding work, order, and discipline; and the need in 5 to monitor that. I refer to those last matters, just to refresh the Court's memory on the matter. If we go to the instructions that come with this document, at page 3 of the exhibit, and this was issued in August 1993 about how to set up the garrisons, and they were at various orders of tasks to be performed, as well as the other jobs that had to be done within the garrison. In summary form, is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that's what the document states so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see in 1 that prepared documents for the organisation of work, order, and discipline following their return to their garrison's territory, that was something that was required to be done in advance, so far as it could be. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But it is not, for example, I mean, to answer the question you asked earlier, whether or not the Knin garrison could be a well functioning body on the 6th of August, in a military organisation, these procedures and these rules are standardized, and are most likely common to all garrisons with the exception of some geographic differences. So which means that the rules as such should already have been prepared prior to establishing the garrison. There will be checklists and templates and so on being used, whereby only specific issues or specific details or specific locations may have to -- to be specified at a later moment, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I just stop you there, because have you seen any in relation to Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean specific rules for the functioning of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen such rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Going through the rest of the pages. Page 4, we can see along with arranging swimming, employing military police units, that a procedure needed to be arranged to enable a unit within the garrison to call the military police if it was wanted that they intervened in a case of unrest. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or in any other case where the garrison commanders -- excuse me, garrison commander considers it necessary to have the intervention of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where's that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. We're looking at -- are you and I looking at the same regulations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but you used the expression "unrest," and the document also says "accidents, et cetera when a military police unit is indispensable to establish order and disciplinary in the area of the garrison." I wasn't reading out document. I was just explaining what I had seen or what my understanding was of the garrison's commanders relations with the military police, and when I look at the document, it is actually corresponds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is quite a simple obligation for the garrison commander. He provides something to a standing orders that any unit within the garrison may see on the barracks wall or be in a handbook which is a procedure telling him that if he's got any problems how to call out the military police. It's as simple as that; isn't it? This is standard?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- for the garrison command as such, that the garrison commander establish there is the procedure for the personnel of the garrison command that when they need military police, that they actually know which number to dial, or do you say that the garrison commander does it for all the units in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, he doesn't do it for all the units in the area.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You agree. It is an internal order that when you arrive as a unit into the garrison, that the company commander or whoever knows how to get in touch with the military police. It's as simple as that; isn't it? It's standard.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But you would as a company commander who is not familiar with the area and who is planning to move there, one would expect -- I mean, it is among the basics of how the military works, that he collects that information prior to arriving in the garrison or in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's why the garrison commander has to write a procedure in advance.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Or there has to be somebody at the -- in the office of the garrison with a telephone and whereby the number is known to the people outside the garrison commander -- outside the garrison command and whereby that somebody can answer questions, like that one, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a call-out. Turning now to the Code of Military Discipline and Article 26; English page 9. This is -- I've got it as 65 ter 1834, but I know it's P1007. And it's the Code of Military Discipline that you have been already discussing, dated May 1992, Article 26, is the one that refers to commanders of units, institutions and garrisons, et cetera, "shall issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of their organic unit, if such measures are required for maintaining order and discipline." Disciplinary measures, just for referencing the matter, in Article 6 are defined as mild violations of the rules. Article 10 has minor breaches of military discipline and the various punishments. And so Article 26, when we look at it, this refers to when an offender is brought before the garrison commander for breach of discipline, and there is an issue to be dealt with as a disciplinary measure. That's right; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. And I think, more specifically, if this offender is not a part or member of the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. And let's take our example of the bridge and the speed limit, and someone breaching the 30-kilometre-per-hour-limit who may be taken to the garrison commander, offender brought before him, explained -- asked for an explanation, and he may deal with it by one of those disciplinary measures, Article 6, and Article 10 in that way. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And, of course, Article 26 applies to, eh?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is why I'm talking this as Article 26, just so we know exactly what we're dealing with here in relation to the authority of the garrison commander. Just turning to some other aspects concerning legal provisions so that we deal with everything as one, if we could see page 86 of your report, and it's page 86 of part 1, and you refer there to the military police administration document of the 17th of December, 1992. And you cite the rules from that document. And I'm reminded your report is P1113, Exhibit P1113.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 86 of -- I don't -- it's not the one I see on the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the screen. That's page 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've got it, though, Mr. Theunens, haven't you. Because you have your report there. You have a look at it as it comes up. There we are. We see it on the page there for Your Honours. Because you cite this matter and refer to these regulations. We can see what you cite from it. You refer to a marked vertical subordination and an effective horizontal coordination. You refer to other passages of the document on page 86. Turning now to page 87, you refer to the garrison commanders, page 3 -- paragraph 3 and 4 on the screen now, and you cite from that document: "Commanders of Croatian army units and garrison commanders are in charge of the military police units operating in their zones of responsibility." You cite further matters. And in paragraph 4, you refer to garrison commanders again. Were you aware you aware that this document was repealed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am indeed aware of that, but I included the document because it actually provided additional background to what is stipulated in the 1994 military police rules, which are P880 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will be looking at them, but I want to take this in stages.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why isn't it in your report that these rules were repealed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it seemed logical to me that when you have a more recent military regulation, that that automatically supercedes or replaces the older regulation, and that is also how I worded it on the English page 86. So the 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn back to page 86 so that can you show the Judges.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the title (B) between brackets the 1994 rules and so on confirm the subordination relations that were established through ... and that is the old document then. It is correct that I didn't explicitly put that the 1994 rules replace the 1992 document, but for me that was logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, the 1994 rules do not contain those provisions about the garrison commands that you have cited in your report. Isn't that right? The 1994 rules is Article 8 and Article 9, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, do you think that that could have been misleading --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to the Court who may be relying upon you for an explanation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 9 states: "While performing their regular military police tasks, MP units are subordinated to the commander of the Military District. The commander of the HRM, which stands for Croatian navy, the commander of the HRZ, which stands for Croatian air force, or the highest ranking HV commander in the military police units area of operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, we see that you cite garrison commanders, and would I be correct in saying that you cited garrison commanders in page 87 of your report, because you are dealing with a case against a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am citing the garrison commander from the 1992 document, which you can see on page 87, and the text is in italics, and it originates from the 1992 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just turn to page 87 while you're referring it so that Their Honours can see it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So -- if we go to the top of the page, the reference to garrison commander is in italics. It is between quotation marks, so it originates from the 1992 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just stop there. Was that extracted because you are dealing with a case against a garrison commander, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not extracted from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Turning to 4, you refer to the bottom three lines of subparagraph 4: "Subordinated to relevant garrison commanders, commanders of relevant HV Guards Brigades, et cetera." Was that cited because you are dealing with a case against a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is cited in order to identify the relevant aspects of this 1992 document. Because the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you said yourself a few days ago, once a new law is into place, the old law is replaced. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not going to give a general opinion in relation to legislation, but I know for military documents and regulations that is the case, and that will also be specified most of the times as such in the new military regulation, i.e., there will be a paragraph at the end or in the beginning stating that this new regulations replaces all other regulations -- older regulations, I'm sorry, in order to avoid any misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you didn't cite these rules of the 17th of December, 1992 as having been imposed as temporary rules under the temporary instructions for the work of the units of the military police of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 3106, if that could be brought up as the first page. There we are. It's just coming on the screen. The temporary instructions for the work of the units of the military police of the Croatian army dated January 1992, exhibit 65 ter 3106, were the temporary rules that can -- that caused those 1992 rules to be made, were you aware of that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember seeing this document before. I may have seen it, but I have not referred to these temporary instructions in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were aware of this document, because -- first of all, were you aware you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clear recollection. So, I mean, if I have to say yes or no, I will say no. I think I have seen them, but I have not used them in my report, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you realize those 1992 rules that you cited in your report at pages 86 and 87 were invoked because of the temporary rules of January 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this specific relation between these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can 65 ter 3106 be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will now move to Exhibit P880, which is the governing rules of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that is Articles 8 and 9 that Mr. Misetic put before you in his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the record, just so that everyone knows, the 1992 rules were repealed under Article 77 of the 1994 rules. We have no need to go there and waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it is Article 8 and 9 which govern the relationship between the military police, under command and control. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And as I have explained, the relations that are established in Articles 8 and 9 are also known as the professional line and the operational line. And that can be found in 65 ter 1336, which is explained on English page 130 of part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we get up exhibit, then, 65 ter 3116 while we're there, if it can be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- that's after the liberation of Knin. So this was passed in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there anything in force before October 1995 called the direct line and professional line?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a specific regulation, but the command and control relations that are established here, are -- did also exist, for example, in the JNA. They also exist in other armies. So based on my background, I concluded that even though the document dates from October 1995, the information that is included in it also applied to the situation that existed prior to October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on what date did it come into effect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we have the corresponding English page of the B/C/S page that is now visible on the screen, we may be able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe that's a little bit difficult to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But is that essential for to us look at, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you wanted to have, like, the exact date. But regulation -- regulation dated from October 1995, and I have explained why I consider that the information included in it also applies to the situation prior to October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And does it apply to the military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and control relationship that is established by Articles 8 and 9 actually corresponds with what is in this regulation described as the -- on the one hand, the professional line, or functional line, and, on the other hand, the operational or direct line. And it applies not only to the military police but also to specialized services like SIS and political affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just turning to Articles 8 and 9, those are the governing Articles relating to the issue of subordination of the military police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that is correct. I mean 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn now to Exhibit D35. Before this became an exhibit in the case, was this a document that you had seen in your preparations? Exhibit D35 is the order issued by the Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak, on the 6th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hadn't seen it prior to becoming an exhibit, but I have reviewed and we discussed it, and we discussed it also with Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any reason why you hadn't seen it before it became an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The only conclusion I can draw is that it didn't pop up in the searchs that I did, and I was very surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at those searches, is that how things happen, that they pop up?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kay, that is not how it happens. But just to explain, for example, when you do searches on numbers of documents, for some reason a number of translated documents put the text handwritten when the number is handwritten, the number of the document. So when I would do a search like, for example, here on 512?, 01?, 94?, 2897, that would not give a hit in English if the number had been put in handwritten. Of course, I checked that for as many documents as I could, but it is a human process. Humans are not perfect unfortunately, and I am afraid that this one of the document I missed due to imperfection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree it's an important document regarding the issuing of orders to the military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an important document, I agree, but it doesn't change what is stipulated in Articles 8 and 9 of P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what it deals with, because there were ambiguities in the system of command and control over the military police units, set out a procedure regarding the issuing of orders. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. For the largest party D35 reiterates was is stipulated in Articles 8 and 9 of P880. Of interest, I mean, in addition to the other paragraphs is paragraph 5 here which describes the procedure in case of conflict of authority between an operational commander and a military police unit commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is it the last document in this section, Your Honour, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have one and a half minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in 10, if we look at page 2 in the English: "All orders regulating the system of command of VP units or manning of VP units in a manner contrary to the Rules ... shall cease to be in effect." Would you agree that that is a very important clause?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important, and if I remember the document well, it refers to a specific situation described in the introduction of this order, whether there seems to have been a problem on the southern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it would be right under your rules of interpretation, as you say, that this coming after the main rules, this would assist in interpreting the main rules and was issued by the minister of defence for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If I had known that we had the document, I would have certainly included it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes this section of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Theunens, I would like to issue the same instructions that I did before; that is, not to speak to anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We would like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past two. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, 2nd of December, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.
